FPB Draft Online Regulation Bill

By: James Carroll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A new set of regulations threatens the very essence of our internet freedom

Summary:
A proposed policy to regulate online content in South Africa is poised to return the country to a worrisome state of severely curtailed free expression. The Draft Online Regulation Policy proposed by the Film and Publication Board (FPB) of South Africa is far-reaching and absolute in its censorship, potentially setting South Africa back by decades on issues of free expression, as well as putting the country on par with some of the world’s worst offenders—like Iran and China—in terms of restrictive legal environments for online speech.

The Draft Online Regulation Policy, introduced by the FPB to regulate commercial content like films and games published online, is a purported attempt to protect children from offensive and illegal content, including child pornography, hate speech, racism, and extreme violence. But the online content covered by this policy would extend beyond that produced by commercial film and game publishers to include content created by individuals who publish game code, post YouTube videos, and ostensibly even those who post content on social media.



Further information:
FURTHER INFORMATION:
A campaign is being led by local awareness group Right 2 Know. We will be speaking to Micah Reddy who is leading the charge in getting clarity of the draft legislation. Justine Limpitlaw, an independent lawyer and author of the Media Law Handbook for Southern Africa will be weighing in and giving her opinion as to why the wording of the policy is so dangerous. Internet Solutions, one of South Africa's largest internet providers, is nervous that they could be fingered as "content producers" and are therefore liable to be billed by the FPB - an amount of up to R750,000 per year. The current draft is contradictory to the Telecoms Act that doesn't allow service providers to "sniff" the contents of their users traffic. Content producers like Gareth Cliff and Suzette would also be directly affected and liable for fees on everything from tweets, Facebook posts, podcasts and short form videos. International Internet watchdog the Electronic Freedom Foundation will also be giving a statement about the parallels between China's policy and South Africa's proposed policy. In further developing news Communications Minister Faith Muthambi recently met with officials in China to to attend a workshop on "development and management of radio and television media for developing countries".
China's government is notorious for its intolerance of a critical, independent media and goes so far as to control what may or may not appear as results for Internet search engines. The government's news agency quotes Muthambi saying: "This visit serves as a good opportunity to learn more about China and its development in broadcast and the broader TV industry. It is also meant to lay a foundation for further exchange and cooperation in these fields between the two countries.”

Is 2015 the year South Africa turns into 1984?

Press Release:


FPB Draft Bill
A proposed policy to regulate online content in South Africa is poised to return the country to a worrisome state of severely curtailed free expression. The Draft Online Regulation Policy proposed by the Film and Publication Board (FPB) is far-reaching and absolute in its censorship, with little clarity on practical implementation. But the FPB is determined to monitor posts on YouTube, blogs and on other forms of social media from April 2016. Are we about to return to the dark ages of enforced censorship? Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Every minute 1380 Blog Posts Are Made

Every minute 120 Hours of Video is Uploaded to Youtube

Every minute 41 000 Photos are Uploaded to Instgram

CLAIRE: The Film and Publication Board’s Draft Online Regulation policy has been called Africa’s Worst Internet Censorship Law – could 2015 become 1984?

CLAIRE VO: In March this year, the Film and Publication Board gazetted a notice inviting public comment on a Draft Online Regulation policy that sought sweeping new powers to effectively police and regulate all aspects of content on the Internet.

CLAIRE VO: In this draft policy the FPB seeks to classify all manner of content, including, for instance, user-submitted videos to sites such as YouTube, which would on paper, require everything to first be classified by the FPB at a charge, and labeled as FPB-approved before it would be allowed to be legally published. The Draft policy was met with very mixed comments and heavy criticism with nearly 9000 protest signatures.But what exactly is the motivation for this new policy in the first place?

THEMBA: Over the years there has been an increase in a number of undesirable content that is happening online: issues of child pornography and lately we’re seeing a lot of racism that is coming online and there’s a lot of bullying that is coming online. And we had to then come up with a policy to try and intervene in this space.

CLAIRE: So what is the intention of the policy?

THEMBA: Let’s start with the mandate of Film and Publications Board, our mandate is basically to regulate. And though quite a number of people would say ‘no your mandate is to censor’, our mandate is to regulate. Otherwise it becomes free for all, and when it becomes free for all, then you have got anarchy. Once you have got anarchy, you are in serious trouble.

CLAIRE VO: Spearheading the online protest against the Draft policy is the Right2Know Campaign, a freedom of expression and access to information movement.

MICAH: What the FPB is trying to do is to give itself sweeping powers, powers that it doesn’t have in terms of the law, to regulate online content and in effect to censor online content. So what they’re trying to do is basically to impose a regime of pre-classification censorship, whereby the role of censoring will effectively be outsourced, outsourced to distributers and publishers. And the term ‘distributor’/ ‘publisher’, as it’s used in the regulations, is so broad that it could include you and me even. It could include blogs, social media sites and so on. And what distributors will be expected to do is to classify all their content in accordance with the Board’s regulations before publishing. So this is a system of what is referred to as ‘prior restraint’.

JUSTINE: the concept of pre-classifying a publication before you give it our to people to consume, is a violation of the constitutional right to freedom of expression and the right of all of us to receive information and expression and ideas.

CLAIRE VO: Justine Limpitlaw is an Electronic Media Law consultant and visiting adjunct professor at the LINK centre at Wits University.

JUSTINE: The Film and Publications Act started off as just that, looking at films and publications. The only kind of publication that needs to be pre-classified is, just for example, child pornography, hate speech, propaganda for war, explicit sex – and that’s when it’s coupled with violence for example or degrading treatment of people.

CLAIRE: Do you believe in online regulations in any form?

MICAH: We acknowledge that there is harmful content online, of course, and we wouldn’t want it to be seen as going against the interests of protecting children; that would be absurd. What the Film and Publications Board is doing though is really heavy-handed and amounts to a sort of blanket-censorship regime – they will call it classification, fine, but the effect as I said just now is censorship, pre-publication censorship.

JUSTINE: One of the most problematic aspects is Section 7 of the draft regulation slash policy, which empowers the Film and Publications Board to take down anything online that it deems harmful or potentially disturbing to children.

GARETH CLIFF: I think it is appalling that people would drop to the depths of putting their children as human shields before freedom of expression. As if freedom of expression can hurt children. These are the same people who probably don’t tell their children the truth about sex or violence or the country that they live in. And I think it’s a problem. I think the biggest problem is that there are people who want to use children as an excuse to put their own narrow-minded myopic conservative agenda in front of everybody else and in front of our constitution. And how dare they?

CLAIRE VO: Always outspoken, former terrestrial radio host Gareth Cliff now runs Cliff Central, an internet based media outlet – that has it’s own policy regarding standards.

GARETH: if you are going to go with censorship, you have to decide who the censor will be, and no one in this room or any other room is going to pick someone else to be their censor.

CLAIRE LINK: Google and other online services have standards and regulations but the Government and FPB feel they need another tier of assessment.

THEMBA: Google does not have the power of the state; it’s a commercial invention. It can just simply download things, block them and so forth. But it cannot prosecute, it cannot say legal frameworks.

JUSTINE: you can’t make for legally binding obligations and certainly can’t purport to impose fines in a policy. And they’ve repeatedly confirmed that this is a policy, just a policy. If they wanted to make legally binding regulations, they can do that, but then they’ve got to fall squarely within the ambit of the Act but the regulations fall so far outside what’s authorized under the Act – they’re not just illegal for being out of the Film and Publications Act, I think they’re unconstitutional for at least 5 to 8 different grounds.

CLAIRE VO: In the interim, the Draft Policy has gained the attention of The Electronic Frontier Foundation in San Francisco, the leading nonprofit organization defending civil liberties in the digital world. Jeremy Malcolm, a native Australian, is the Senior Global Policy Analyst for the group. Should the draft policy become reality, he feels there could be more far reaching repercussions.

JEREMY: Well, the most obvious thing that is definitely going to happen is that we’re going to be seeing South African businesses going overseas to host their material. This has been seen in other countries around the world. When Australia brought in some tougher censorship legislation there were websites that simply relocated overseas, the jobs went overseas, the jobs associated with those websites went overseas and now they are beyond the Australian governments control. This is the same of what we expect to happen in South Africa – there are more countries that are friendlier towards free speech and have higher levels of protection for internet companies and every incentive is going to send South African entrepreneurs and innovators to those countries.

CLAIRE: what are your timelines in terms of implementing this policy?

THEMBA: Next year, I want it kicking in April next year.

CLAIRE: Is that feasible?

THEMBA: Yes it is, because we’ve done quite a lot of consultations, we have spent this whole year on consultations. So we know we have got the content, we’ll improve that content and we have got about 6 months.

JUSTINE: Just think about how much content is on the internet. I’m not joking, there are only 55 million South Africans, I mean if every single one of them was employed by the Film and Publications Board, I’m not sure they could keep up with the information that’s getting uploaded onto the internet all the time.

CLAIRE (LINK): At this stage there is no indication of the costs involved and even less clarity of where the money will go.

CLAIRE VO: At the moment, it can take the FPB up to two weeks to classify a feature film.

MICAH: so this is the same Film and Publications Board that tried to censor The Spear, the famous painting of course, which was a legitimate work of art, it was a legitimate piece of political satire. This is also the same Film and Publications Board that tried to censor the film of Good Report. Durban International Film Festival was going to run it, and the FPB said ‘no, this contains child porn’. It wasn’t child porn at all, it was actually a very serious film about a very serious issue, which is relationships between school girls and male teachers, it’s a very serious issue in South African society, and it explored it in a very critical way.

JUSTINE: No democratic country with serious constitutional credentials has ventured into this territory, none. We need to be very careful about who we want to associate.

JEREMY: The way it works in countries like Saudi Arabia and China is that they will stop 90% of what they want to stop but there will always be 10% that goes through. There will always be people who really want to gain access to something that has been prohibited just because it has been prohibited, it’s kind of a challenge and they are able to find ways to do that. I mean, you have to ask two questions, firstly is this going to clamp down on legitimate expression online and is it even going to be effective in dealing with the problematic expression that they are trying to curb?

GARETH: it won’t be enforceable. And just like so many other things that the government can’t get right, it will just be another thing they don’t do properly. And they’ll try, and there’ll be one or two cases that will have to go to court because that’s the only place you can get the government to see what they’re doing is wrong. And ultimately freedom of expression will win because people can’t be silenced anymore. Governments can’t control us anymore. This is the best time to be alive.

CLAIRE VO: At the moment, it can take the FPB up to two weeks to classify a feature film. MICAH: so this is the same Film and Publications Board that tried to censor The Spear, the famous painting of course, which was a legitimate work of art, it was a legitimate piece of political satire. This is also the same Film and Publications Board that tried to censor the film of Good Report. Durban International Film Festival was going to run it, and the FPB said ‘no, this contains child porn’. It wasn’t child porn at all, it was actually a very serious film about a very serious issue, which is relationships between school girls and male teachers, it’s a very serious issue in South African society, and it explored it in a very critical way. JUSTINE: No democratic country with serious constitutional credentials has ventured into this territory, none. We need to be very careful about who we want to associate. JEREMY: The way it works in countries like Saudi Arabia and China is that they will stop 90% of what they want to stop but there will always be 10% that goes through. There will always be people who really want to gain access to something that has been prohibited just because it has been prohibited, it’s kind of a challenge and they are able to find ways to do that. I mean, you have to ask two questions, firstly is this going to clamp down on legitimate expression online and is it even going to be effective in dealing with the problematic expression that they are trying to curb? GARETH: it won’t be enforceable. And just like so many other things that the government can’t get right, it will just be another thing they don’t do properly. And they’ll try, and there’ll be one or two cases that will have to go to court because that’s the only place you can get the government to see what they’re doing is wrong. And ultimately freedom of expression will win because people can’t be silenced anymore. Governments can’t control us anymore. This is the best time to be alive. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A new set of regulations threatens the very essence of our internet freedom
metadata.Summary: A proposed policy to regulate online content in South Africa is poised to return the country to a worrisome state of severely curtailed free expression. The Draft Online Regulation Policy proposed by the Film and Publication Board (FPB) of South Africa is far-reaching and absolute in its censorship, potentially setting South Africa back by decades on issues of free expression, as well as putting the country on par with some of the world’s worst offenders—like Iran and China—in terms of restrictive legal environments for online speech. The Draft Online Regulation Policy, introduced by the FPB to regulate commercial content like films and games published online, is a purported attempt to protect children from offensive and illegal content, including child pornography, hate speech, racism, and extreme violence. But the online content covered by this policy would extend beyond that produced by commercial film and game publishers to include content created by individuals who publish game code, post YouTube videos, and ostensibly even those who post content on social media.
metadata.Further information: FURTHER INFORMATION: A campaign is being led by local awareness group Right 2 Know. We will be speaking to Micah Reddy who is leading the charge in getting clarity of the draft legislation. Justine Limpitlaw, an independent lawyer and author of the Media Law Handbook for Southern Africa will be weighing in and giving her opinion as to why the wording of the policy is so dangerous. Internet Solutions, one of South Africa's largest internet providers, is nervous that they could be fingered as "content producers" and are therefore liable to be billed by the FPB - an amount of up to R750,000 per year. The current draft is contradictory to the Telecoms Act that doesn't allow service providers to "sniff" the contents of their users traffic. Content producers like Gareth Cliff and Suzette would also be directly affected and liable for fees on everything from tweets, Facebook posts, podcasts and short form videos. International Internet watchdog the Electronic Freedom Foundation will also be giving a statement about the parallels between China's policy and South Africa's proposed policy. In further developing news Communications Minister Faith Muthambi recently met with officials in China to to attend a workshop on "development and management of radio and television media for developing countries". China's government is notorious for its intolerance of a critical, independent media and goes so far as to control what may or may not appear as results for Internet search engines. The government's news agency quotes Muthambi saying: "This visit serves as a good opportunity to learn more about China and its development in broadcast and the broader TV industry. It is also meant to lay a foundation for further exchange and cooperation in these fields between the two countries.” Is 2015 the year South Africa turns into 1984?
